mainTopic: Neighbors' rights in shared and public space: sealing windows, openings and privacy in a partners' courtyard, and digging under or building over רשות הרבים.
overview: This amud begins by finishing a rule about חזקה: if someone seals a neighbor's window in front of him and the neighbor stays silent, the right to keep it sealed is set right away. The גמרא then explains that a newly bought house may not open into a partners' courtyard because it adds traffic. רב הונא explains that the end of that משנה only allows dividing space the house already has. A new משנה forbids opening a door or window directly facing a neighbor's in a shared courtyard, or enlarging or adding openings, but allows all of this toward רשות הרבים. רבי יוחנן finds the source in בלעם praising ישראל because their tent doors did not face each other. רבא rejects רמי בר חמא's idea that the rule is about courtyard space and shows it is about privacy. Toward the public street the rule does not apply, because the neighbor already has to hide from passersby. Another משנה forbids digging under רשות הרבים or building projections out over it. In a story, רבי אמי orders a man to cut off his projection and explains that an alleyway's residents can give up their claim, but no one can give up the public's claim. A similar story about רבי ינאי and a leaning tree begins and continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Sealing a window creates an immediate right
steps.stepSummary: If one person seals another's window while he watches, a חזקה is set at once, because nobody stays quiet while his light is blocked.
steps.simpleTranslation: And for sealing a window, a חזקה is set immediately, because a person does not usually stay silent while his light is being blocked in front of him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes a rule from the earlier discussion. Sealing a window creates a חזקה right away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usually a חזקה needs time to build up. Here it is immediate, because staying silent in this case shows the owner agreed or that the other person had the right. People do not keep quiet while their light is taken away in front of them.

keyTerms.meaning: An established legal right or presumption
To seal or close up (here, a window)

phrases.english: And to seal – it is a חזקה immediately,
phrases.notes: This means sealing someone else's window while he is watching.

phrases.english: for a person is not accustomed
to have his light sealed in front of him and stay silent.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the earlier discussion of window rights from the previous daf.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sealing another's window in his presence establishes a חזקה immediately, because his silence shows agreement or permission.

steps.title: Why may a new house not open into the partners' courtyard?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the earlier משנה about a house bought in a neighboring courtyard and asks for its reason.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone bought a house in a different courtyard, he may not open it into the partners' courtyard. What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic by quoting a line from the משנה. It asks why the rule is so, which sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The case is a person who owns a share in one courtyard and buys a house in the courtyard next to it. The משנה says he cannot make a door from that house into the first, shared courtyard. The גמרא wants the reason, because the reason will decide how far the rule reaches.

keyTerms.meaning: A courtyard owned jointly by partners

phrases.english: If he bought a house in another courtyard –
he may not open it into the partners' courtyard.
What is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to a new line of the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason a newly bought house in a neighboring courtyard may not open into the shared courtyard.

steps.title: Because it adds traffic
steps.stepSummary: The reason is that the new door brings more people walking through the shared courtyard.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because he increases the traffic on them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the reason: opening the new house would bring more people walking through the partners' courtyard.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The other partners have a right not to have more people crossing their courtyard than before. A new door from another house means new residents and more coming and going. Keep this reason in mind, because the next step uses it to question the end of the משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: Increases traffic or foot traffic on them

phrases.english: Because he increases the traffic on them.
phrases.notes: "Them" means the other partners in the courtyard.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 2.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The rule exists because more people would walk through the shared courtyard.

steps.title: But the end of the משנה allows building more rooms
steps.stepSummary: The משנה lets him build a room inside his house or an upper floor on top of it. That should also add traffic.
steps.simpleTranslation: Look at the end of the משנה: if he wants, he may build a room inside his house or an upper floor on top of his house. But doesn't that also increase the traffic?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the reason it just gave. The end of the משנה seems to allow something that would also add traffic.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the concern is more people crossing the courtyard, then a new room or upper floor could also house more people. Yet the משנה allows it. So either the reason is wrong, or the room and upper floor need a different explanation.

keyTerms.meaning: Say (look at) the last part of the משנה

phrases.english: Say the last clause:
Rather, if he wants –
he builds a room inside his house,
and builds an upper floor on top of his house.
But doesn't he increase the traffic on him!
phrases.notes: "Him" means the other partner in the courtyard.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reason given in step 3, using the end of the same משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reason that added traffic is forbidden.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The end of the משנה permits a new room or upper floor, which would also add traffic, so the reason seems to contradict the משנה.

steps.title: רב הונא: only dividing space that already exists
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא explains that the "room" means splitting an existing room in two, and the "upper floor" means an inner story built inside existing space.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא said: what does "room" mean? That he divided a room into two. And what does "upper floor" mean? An inner story.
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא answers the challenge. The משנה only allows rearranging space the house already has, which does not add new traffic.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Splitting an existing room, or adding a floor inside the existing height, does not really make the house bigger. So it brings no more people than before, and the reason of added traffic still stands. The permission at the end of the משנה is limited to these cases.

keyTerms.meaning: That he divided it in two
An inner story made by dividing existing space

steps.whatToRemember: No new traffic in a partners' courtyard: you may not open a newly bought house into it, but you may rearrange the space already inside your own house.

phrases.english: רב הונא said:
What is a "room"? That he divided it in two,
and what is an "upper floor"? An inner story.
phrases.notes: Here it means an extra level built inside the house's existing space, not a new floor added on top.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 4.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the terms of the משנה's case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה lets him add a brand-new room or story, which would add traffic.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה only allows dividing existing space, which adds no traffic.

steps.title: No facing doors or windows in a shared courtyard
steps.stepSummary: The new משנה forbids opening a door or window directly facing a neighbor's in a shared courtyard, and forbids enlarging an opening or adding a second one.
steps.simpleTranslation: A person may not open into a partners' courtyard a door facing another door, or a window facing another window. If his opening was small, he may not make it big. If there was one, he may not make it two.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It protects the privacy of people who share a courtyard by limiting new openings.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A door or window directly across from a neighbor's lets one person see into the other's home. Making an opening bigger or adding another one also increases how much the neighbor can be seen. So the partners can block these changes.

keyTerms.meaning: The משנה (marks the start of a new משנה)
A door directly facing another door

phrases.english: MISHNA:
A person may not open into a partners' courtyard
a door facing a door
or a window facing a window.
If it was small – he may not make it big,
if it was one – he may not make it two.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new משנה, separate from the previous discussion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In a shared courtyard, one may not open a door or window facing another's, enlarge an opening, or add a second one.

steps.title: Toward the public domain, everything is allowed
steps.stepSummary: Toward רשות הרבים, a person may open facing doors and windows, enlarge an opening, and add more.
steps.simpleTranslation: But toward the public domain he may open a door facing a door and a window facing a window. If it was small, he may make it big. If there was one, he may make it two.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives the other side of its rule. Facing the public street, none of these limits apply.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In רשות הרבים, people are already seen by everyone walking by, so there is no private space to protect. That is why all the limits from the shared courtyard fall away. The גמרא spells out this reason in step 14.

keyTerms.meaning: The public domain, such as a street

steps.whatToRemember: In a shared courtyard, privacy is protected: no facing openings, no enlarging, no adding. Toward the public street, all of these are allowed.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix this up with the earlier rule about traffic. This משנה is about privacy and seeing into a neighbor's home, not about more people walking through.

phrases.english: But he may open into the public domain
a door facing a door
and a window facing a window.
If it was small – he may make it big,
and if one – he may make it two.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Contrasts the public domain with the shared courtyard of step 6.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Toward the public domain, facing openings, enlarging an opening, and adding openings are all permitted.

steps.title: Where does the rule against facing doorways come from?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens by asking for the source of the משנה's rule that a person may not open a door facing his neighbor's door.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: From where do we know these rules?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins discussing the משנה by asking for a source. This sets up the next step, where an answer is given.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה said a person may not open a doorway or window directly facing a neighbor's in a shared courtyard. The גמרא wants to know what this is based on, since the משנה gave no source.

keyTerms.meaning: The discussion that explains the משנה
From where do we know these things? (a request for a source)

phrases.english: GEMARA: From where are these matters derived?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the גמרא on the new משנה quoted in steps 6 and 7.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source for the rule against facing doorways in a shared courtyard.

steps.title: בלעם saw that the tents of ישראל did not face each other
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן brings the פסוק in which בלעם sees ישראל dwelling by tribes. The tent doors did not face each other, so ישראל was worthy of the שכינה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן says: The פסוק says, "And בלעם lifted his eyes and saw ישראל dwelling by its tribes." What did he see? He saw that the doorways of their tents did not face each other. He said: These people are worthy of having the שכינה rest on them.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן answers the question with a פסוק about בלעם. בלעם noticed that no tent door faced another one, and he praised ישראל for it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words "dwelling by its tribes" are read as describing how the tents were set up: each family had privacy, with no doors facing each other. Since this kind of privacy is praised as making ישראל worthy of the שכינה, it becomes the source for the משנה's rule.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that the rule is not only about property rights. It is built on the value of privacy and modesty, which the Torah praises.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yoḥanan says: Because the verse states:
"And Balaam lifted up his eyes,
and he saw Israel dwelling tribe by tribe"
What did he see?
He saw that the entrances of their tents were not
lined up facing each other.
He said: These people are worthy
of having the Divine Presence rest upon them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the request for a source in step 8.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק about בלעם seeing ישראל's tents set up so that no doors faced each other.

steps.title: רמי בר חמא's first idea about enlarging a small doorway
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's ban on enlarging a small doorway. רמי בר חמא suggests the reason is that a wider doorway gives its owner more space in the courtyard, so widening is fine if it does not add space.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: "If it was small, he may not make it big." רמי בר חמא wanted to say: A doorway four אמות wide may not be widened to eight, because then he takes eight אמות in the courtyard. But widening a doorway two אמות wide to four is fine.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a line from the משנה, and רמי בר חמא offers his explanation of it. This sets up רבא's response in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רמי בר חמא thinks the problem is about rights to courtyard space: a wider door claims more space in front of it. A doorway of two אמות already gets four אמות of space, so widening it to four adds nothing and should be allowed by his reasoning.

keyTerms.meaning: He thought to say (an idea that will later be rejected)
A cubit, a unit of length (plural: אַמּוֹת)

steps.confusionAlert: "סבר רמי בר חמא למימר" means "he thought to say". It warns you that this idea is about to be rejected, so do not treat it as the final הלכה.

phrases.english: If it was small, he may not make it large.
Rami bar Ḥama thought to say:

phrases.aramaic: בַּר אַרְבְּעֵי לָא לִישַׁוְּיֵיהּ בַּר תְּמָנְיָא –
phrases.english: A doorway of four may not be made into one of eight,
phrases.notes: The numbers are אמות of width.

phrases.english: because he would take eight in the courtyard.
phrases.notes: He assumes a doorway gives its owner use of the courtyard space in front of it, as wide as the door, and at least four אמות.

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל בַּר תַּרְתֵּי לִישַׁוְּיֵיהּ בַּר אַרְבְּעֵי –
phrases.english: But to make a doorway of two into one of four
is perfectly fine.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the source of the rule to explaining the next clause of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Proposed reading: enlarging a doorway is banned only when it adds courtyard space; widening from two to four אמות is allowed.

steps.title: רבא: a bigger doorway takes away the neighbor's privacy
steps.stepSummary: רבא rejects רמי בר חמא's idea. The neighbor can object because he can hide from a small doorway but not from a large one.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to him: The neighbor can say to him, "With a small doorway I can hide from you. With a big doorway I cannot hide from you."
steps.whatsHappening: רבא rejects רמי בר חמא's explanation. He says the real problem with a wider doorway is privacy, not courtyard space.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even if widening adds no courtyard space, a wider opening lets the owner see more of what the neighbor does. So any enlargement can be stopped, even from two אמות to four.

keyTerms.meaning: He can say to him (the neighbor has a valid claim)
To hide oneself, to keep private

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבָא, מָצֵי אָמַר לֵיהּ:
phrases.english: Rava said to him: The neighbor can say to him:
With a small entrance I can conceal myself from you;

phrases.aramaic: בְּפִיתְחָא רַבָּה לָא מָצֵינָא אִצְטְנוֹעֵי מִינָּךְ.
phrases.english: with a large entrance I cannot conceal myself from you.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבָא, מָצֵי אָמַר לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects רמי בר חמא's reasoning in step 10.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the reason (courtyard space) and therefore the leniency of widening from two to four אמות.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The issue is privacy, which any enlargement harms, not only extra courtyard space.

steps.title: רמי בר חמא's same idea about splitting one doorway into two
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's ban on making one doorway into two. רמי בר חמא again says the reason is extra courtyard space, so splitting is fine when it adds no space.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: "If there was one, he may not make it two." רמי בר חמא wanted to say: A doorway four אמות wide may not be made into two doorways of two אמות each, because then he takes eight אמות in the courtyard. But an eight-אמה doorway made into two of four each is fine.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה, and רמי בר חמא uses the same courtyard-space reasoning. This sets up רבא's response.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each doorway gets at least four אמות of courtyard space. Splitting a four-אמה door into two small ones would double his space to eight, but splitting an eight-אמה door into two four-אמה doors keeps the same eight, so he thinks that is allowed.

phrases.english: If there was one, he may not make it into two.
Rami bar Ḥama thought to say:
A doorway of four may not be made
into two doorways of two each,
because he would take eight in the courtyard.
phrases.notes: Each doorway gets four אמות in front of it, so two doorways get eight.

phrases.english: But to make a doorway of eight
into doorways of four each is perfectly fine.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the same reasoning from step 10 to the next clause of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Proposed reading: splitting a doorway is banned only when it adds courtyard space.

steps.title: רבא: two doorways take away more privacy than one
steps.stepSummary: רבא rejects the idea again. The neighbor can hide from one doorway but not from two.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to him: The neighbor can say, "With one doorway I can hide from you. With two I cannot hide from you."
steps.whatsHappening: רבא rejects רמי בר חמא's explanation a second time, again pointing to privacy.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two doorways give two different views into the neighbor's area, even if the total width stays the same. So splitting a doorway can always be stopped.
steps.whatToRemember: In both cases רבא teaches that the rules about doorways in a shared courtyard protect privacy (היזק ראיה), not rights to courtyard space. Any change that adds viewing, whether a wider door or a second door, can be stopped.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבָא, מָצֵי אֲמַר לֵיהּ:
phrases.english: Rava said to him: The neighbor can say to him:
With one entrance I can conceal myself from you;
with two I cannot conceal myself from you.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבָא, מָצֵי אֲמַר לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects רמי בר חמא's reasoning in step 12, the same way as step 11.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the leniency of splitting an eight-אמה doorway into two four-אמה doorways.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: A second opening harms privacy no matter how much courtyard space it claims.

steps.title: Why opening toward the public domain is allowed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's permission to open facing doorways toward רשות הרבים and explains it: the neighbor already has to hide from the public anyway.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: "But he may open a doorway facing another doorway toward the public domain." This is because he can say to the neighbor: "In the end, you already have to hide from the people in the public domain."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the משנה's lenient ruling about רשות הרבים and gives the reason for it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Facing a public street, the neighbor never had privacy to begin with, because people pass by all the time. So a new doorway takes away nothing he had, and the privacy claim does not apply.

keyTerms.meaning: The public domain, a public street

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the limit of the privacy rule: a neighbor can only protect privacy he really has, not privacy he has already lost to the public.

phrases.english: But he may open toward the public domain
an entrance opposite an entrance.
Because he can say to him: In the end,

phrases.aramaic: הָא בָּעֵית אִצְטְנוֹעֵי מִבְּנֵי רְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים.
phrases.english: you must conceal yourself from the people of the public domain anyway.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the privacy reasoning from steps 11 and 13 to explain the משנה's leniency toward the public domain.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Toward רשות הרבים the neighbor has no privacy to lose, since he already must hide from the public.

steps.title: No digging pits or caves under the public domain
steps.stepSummary: The new משנה forbids digging pits, ditches, or caves under רשות הרבים. רבי אליעזר allows it if the covering is strong enough to hold a loaded wagon.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: One may not dig an empty space under the public domain, such as pits, ditches, or caves. רבי אליעזר permits it, as long as it is strong enough that a wagon loaded with stones could travel over it.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins with a new topic: digging hollow spaces underneath public land.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worry is that the ground above could collapse and hurt people walking or driving in public. The תנא קמא forbids it completely. רבי אליעזר allows it when the cover is strong enough that collapse is not a real danger.

keyTerms.meaning: The public domain, land used by everyone
Pits, ditches, and caves: different kinds of dug-out spaces
A wagon loaded with stones, the test of a strong covering

phrases.english: MISHNA: One may not make a hollow space
under the public domain:
pits, ditches, or caves.
Rabbi Eliezer permits it
provided that a wagon could travel over it
even when loaded with stones.
phrases.notes: The text leaves it unsaid, but he means the covering over the hole has to be that strong.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ אֵין עוֹשִׂין חָלָל תַּחַת רְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה on a new topic, moving from doorways in a shared courtyard to digging under public land.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Hollow spaces may not be dug under רשות הרבים. רבי אליעזר permits them if the covering can hold a loaded wagon.

steps.title: No projections or balconies over the public domain
steps.stepSummary: The משנה forbids extending projections or balconies into רשות הרבים, unless the builder first pulls his wall back. A buyer of a courtyard that already has them may keep them.
steps.simpleTranslation: One may not extend projections or balconies into the public domain. If he wants one, he moves his wall back into his own property and then builds it out. If someone bought a courtyard that already had projections and balconies, it keeps its established status.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה continues with a second public-space rule: what may stick out over public land.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A projection over the street takes over public space, so it is not allowed. The fix is to move the wall inward, so the projection only hangs over the owner's own land. A buyer may keep projections that were already there, because the courtyard comes with that established status (חזקה).

keyTerms.meaning: Projections, beams or ledges sticking out from a wall
He pulls back into his own property
In its established status: it may stay as it is

phrases.english: One may not extend projections or balconies
into the public domain.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אִם רָצָה – כּוֹנֵס לְתוֹךְ שֶׁלּוֹ,
phrases.english: Rather, if he wants to, he pulls back into his own property
and extends it.
phrases.notes: He moves his wall inward, so the projection only hangs over his own land.

phrases.english: If he bought a courtyard with projections and balconies on it,
it keeps its established status.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֵין מוֹצִיאִין זִיזִין וּגְזוּזְטְרָאוֹת לִרְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same משנה, moving from digging under public land to building out over it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Projections may not stick out into רשות הרבים unless the wall is moved back first. Existing projections on a purchased courtyard keep their חזקה.

steps.title: Why the Rabbis forbid digging even with a strong cover
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the רבנן's reason is against רבי אליעזר. It answers that a covering can wear away over time without the owner noticing.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: And what is the reasoning of the רבנן? Sometimes the covering wears away, and he does not notice.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why the רבנן disagree with רבי אליעזר, and answers right away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אליעזר's view makes sense: a strong cover means no danger. The רבנן look ahead. Even a strong cover can weaken over time without the owner noticing, and then it could collapse on the public.

keyTerms.meaning: And the רבנן? A short way of asking for their reason
He is not aware of it

phrases.english: GEMARA: And the Rabbis?
phrases.notes: רבי אליעזר's reason is clear. The question is why the רבנן still forbid it when the cover is strong.

phrases.english: Sometimes it wears away
and he is not aware of it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the first ruling of the משנה (step 15) to explain the רבנן's side of the dispute.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What is the רבנן's reason for forbidding digging even when the cover is strong?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A cover can wear away over time without the owner noticing, so it is still dangerous.

steps.title: רבי אמי tells a man to cut off his projection
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's ban on projections and tells a story. The public objected to a man's projection, and רבי אמי, who had a projection of his own over an alleyway, ordered him to cut it off.
steps.simpleTranslation: One may not extend projections and balconies, and so on. רבי אמי had a projection that stuck out into an alleyway. A certain man also had a projection, and his stuck out into the public domain. The people of the public domain were objecting to it. He came before רבי אמי, who told him: Go cut it off.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a real-life case that applies the משנה's ban on projections into רשות הרבים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אמי rules just as the משנה says: a projection over public land must go. The story makes a point of mentioning that רבי אמי had a projection of his own. That detail sets up the man's challenge in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: An alleyway, shared by a small group of residents
They were objecting or holding him back

phrases.english: One may not extend projections and balconies, and so on.
Rabbi Ami had a projection
that stuck out into an alleyway.

phrases.aramaic: וְהַהוּא גַּבְרָא נָמֵי הֲוָה לֵיהּ זִיזָא,
phrases.english: And a certain man also had a projection
that stuck out into the public domain.

phrases.aramaic: הֲווֹ קָא מְעַכְּבִי עֲלֵיהּ בְּנֵי רְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים.
phrases.english: The people of the public domain were objecting to him.
He came before Rabbi Ami.
He said to him: Go cut it off.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי אַמֵּי הֲוָה לֵיהּ זִיזָא דַּהֲוָה נָפֵיק לִמְבוֹאָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the משנה's ban on projections (step 16) to a real case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A projection over רשות הרבים that the public objects to must be cut off.

steps.title: The man points to רבי אמי's own projection
steps.stepSummary: The man challenges רבי אמי: you have a projection too, so why must I remove mine?
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: But the Master also has one!
steps.whatsHappening: The man pushes back: if רבי אמי has a projection himself, how can he order someone else to remove one?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge is that רבי אמי seems to be acting against his own ruling. If projections are forbidden, his should be forbidden too. This sets up רבי אמי's explanation of how the two cases differ.

keyTerms.meaning: But look! It opens a challenge
Master, a respectful way to say 'you'

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: וְהָא מָר נָמֵי אִית לֵיהּ!
phrases.english: He said to him: But the Master also has one!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי אמי's ruling from step 18 by pointing to his own projection.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אמי's order to cut off the man's projection
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי אמי has a projection himself, so he seems to be applying the rule to others but not to himself.

steps.title: An alleyway can give up its claim; the public cannot
steps.stepSummary: רבי אמי answers that his projection is over an alleyway whose residents gave up their claim. No one can give up the claim of רשות הרבים.
steps.simpleTranslation: Mine sticks out into an alleyway, and the alleyway's residents have given up their claim for me. Yours sticks out into the public domain. Who can give up the claim for you?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אמי explains why his projection is allowed and the man's is not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An alleyway belongs to a known, small group of residents, so they can agree to let him keep it (מחילה). רשות הרבים belongs to everyone, including people not even present, so no one has the power to give up the public's claim. The two projections look the same, but the space they hang over makes the difference.

keyTerms.meaning: They give up their claim, waive their right
Who can give up the claim?

steps.whatToRemember: Projections may not stick out over רשות הרבים. A private alleyway's residents can give up their claim and allow one, but nobody can do that on behalf of the public.
steps.confusionAlert: רבי אמי is not saying projections into an alleyway are always allowed. His is allowed only because the alleyway's residents agreed to it.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets out a key difference: rights in shared private space can be given up by its owners, but public rights belong to everyone and cannot be given up by anyone.

phrases.english: Mine sticks out into an alleyway:
phrases.notes: The text doesn't say so, but this is רבי אמי answering the man.

phrases.english: the residents of the alleyway give up their claim for me.
Yours sticks out into the public domain;
who can give up the claim for you?

steps.triggerLanguage: דִּידִי לִמְבוֹאָה מַפֵּיק בְּנֵי מְבוֹאָה מָחֲלִין גַּבַּאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 19 by showing that the two cases are different.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Every projection over shared space is the same, so רבי אמי's projection should be forbidden too.
steps.terutzMaskana: An alleyway's known residents can give up their claim, but no one can give up the claim of רשות הרבים, so only the public projection must go.

steps.title: A second story: a tree leaning over the public street
steps.stepSummary: רבי ינאי owned a tree leaning into רשות הרבים. Another man had one too, and the public protested against him. The man came to רבי ינאי, and the step ends just as רבי ינאי begins to speak.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ינאי had a tree that leaned out over the public street. There was a certain man who also had a tree leaning over the public street. The public came and protested against him. He came before רבי ינאי, and רבי ינאי said to him:
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new story that looks a lot like the רבי אמי story we just learned. This step only sets the scene; רבי ינאי's reply is the next move.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The setup copies the earlier story on purpose. The judge, רבי ינאי, has the very same thing the man is being blamed for: a tree hanging over the public street. So we expect the same question as before ("you have one too!") and wonder how רבי ינאי will handle it.

keyTerms.meaning: A certain man (the usual way the גמרא begins a story about an unnamed person)
They were protesting or objecting against him

steps.confusionAlert: The phrase "said to him" at the end is רבי ינאי speaking to the man, not the man speaking to רבי ינאי. The step stops before we hear what he said.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yannai had
a tree leaning into the public domain.
There was a certain man
who also had
a tree leaning into the public domain,
the people of the public domain came
and were protesting against him.
He came before Rabbi Yannai,
he said to him:
phrases.notes: This is רבי ינאי talking to the man. His words come on the next amud.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יַנַּאי הֲוָה לֵיהּ אִילָן הַנּוֹטֶה לִרְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a second story that parallels the רבי אמי story (Steps 18-20). This time the case is a leaning tree instead of a projection.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: No ruling yet. The step sets up a case where a judge who has a tree over רשות הרבים is asked about another man's tree over רשות הרבים.
